name: Galeri Nasional Indonesia
funding: State gallery owned by Indonesia's Culture Ministry, a ministry created under President Prabowo; before that it sat under the education and culture ministry. Holds 1,770 artworks.
watch: On 19 December 2024 it cancelled Yos Suprapto's show ten minutes before opening after he refused to cover more paintings of Jokowi.
why_flagged: State gallery owned by Indonesia's Culture Ministry, a ministry created under President Prabowo; before that it sat under the education and culture ministry. Holds 1,770 artworks.
records_note: A 2024 ministry performance report covers it only inside a ten-body unit.

overview: State art gallery at Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur 14, Central Jakarta, opposite Gambir Station (Wikipedia; Popmama).
Dedicated as the national gallery on 8 May 1999 (Wikipedia).

The main building, Gedung A, was built in 1817 as a Dutch Indies residence with materials from Kasteel Batavia. From 1900 it housed the Carpentier Alting Stichting school, abolished in 1961. After 1965 it served as a student group's and then an army brigade's headquarters, before returning to the education and culture department in 1981 to 1982 (Wikipedia).
Holds about 1,770 works, including Raden Saleh, Affandi and Basuki Abdullah, and foreign artists such as Wassily Kandinsky, Victor Vasarely and Zao Wou-Ki (Wikipedia).
Jarot Mahendra was named in January 2025 as the person in charge of the gallery unit (Antara).
Open Tuesday to Sunday, 9am to 7pm. Free entry with online registration (Popmama, May 2026).
details.funding_verdict: Galeri Nasional Indonesia: public: Indonesia's Culture Ministry
funding: Owned by the Ministry of Culture through the Indonesian Heritage Agency (Wikipedia), one of the new ministries created in President Prabowo Subianto's cabinet expansion (The Jakarta Post).

It sits inside one public service agency (BLU) with other state museums; in April 2026 Culture Minister Fadli Zon said the gallery should ideally be run as its own BLU, and the head of Museums and Cultural Heritage, Indira Esti Nurjadin, said the units must keep raising non-tax state revenue (RRI).

red_flags.heading: Yos Suprapto exhibition cancelled
points: The gallery asked Yogyakarta artist Yos Suprapto to remove five of 30 paintings from "Kebangkitan: Tanah Untuk Kedaulatan Pangan", works that press reports link to former president Joko Widodo; he covered two, "Konoha I" and "Konoha II", with black cloth and refused to hide three more (ArtAsiaPacific).

Curator Suwarno Wisetrotomo resigned, calling the works "too vulgar"; the gallery called off the show ten minutes before its 19 December 2024 opening, citing "unavoidable technical constraints" (ArtAsiaPacific).
Zamrud Sayta Negara, head of the gallery team, denied any intent to ban the show; Fadli Zon said the five works had no link to food sovereignty and raised a possible political motive (Mongabay).

LBH Jakarta and Komnas HAM criticised the cancellation as a restriction on freedom of expression (Mongabay); on 24 January 2025 Megawati criticised it at a PDI Perjuangan event, saying "ekspresi seni itu harus dihormati" (artistic expression must be respected, our translation) (CNN Indonesia).

press.overall: The criticism centres on the December 2024 cancellation, covered by the art press and as a press-freedom issue by national media.

items.title: Annette Meier, "Indonesian Artist's Exhibition Canceled Over Political Paintings" (2025)
points: Reports the requests to hide the works, the curator's resignation and the cancellation.
Quotes Yos comparing it to censorship and calling it "an alarm for freedom of expression in Indonesia"; notes Fadli Zon withdrew from opening the show.

items.title: editorial board, "Authoritarian alarm" (2025)
points: Argues the closure should alarm the country about free expression and that the gallery "refused to live in the present"; the images spread online anyway.
Sets it beside a broadcasting bill critics said would widen censorship powers.
A national newspaper editorial, not art media; subscription prompts appear, but the full text was readable.

details.bottom_line: The gallery is paid for and run by the state, with no private sponsors on record. The weak point is political control: in 2024 it cancelled a show over paintings that press reports link to Jokowi, and the Culture Minister who oversees it suggested a political motive. Worth watching: how the planned move to its own public service agency changes its independence.

name: Jakarta Biennale
funding: Run since 2024 by Majelis Jakarta, an artist-collective network. 2026 partners: Dulux, Artotel's Paviliun Raden Saleh, iForte. Jakarta culture office and Jakpro logos are unlabelled; no budget published.
watch: Founded 1974 by the Jakarta Arts Council. The 2026 edition, KEBAL, runs 4 Oct to 28 Nov at Taman Ismail Marzuki.
records_note: The partner page shows sponsor and media-partner logos with role labels only.
affiliations_note: Organised by the Majelis Jakarta collective network, with Gudskul Ekosistem and the FSRD IKJ art faculty among its 2026 host spaces. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

overview: Recurring contemporary art exhibition held at Taman Ismail Marzuki (TIM), the Jakarta arts complex, and at collective spaces across the city. The 2024 edition, which ran from 1 October to 15 November, used the Emiria Soenassa and S. Sudjojono galleries at TIM (NOW! Jakarta, Sari Widiati, 31 October 2024).

Its precursor was the Pameran Besar Seni Lukis Indonesia 1974 (Major Exhibition of Indonesian Painting) at TIM. Art school students answered it with the Desember Hitam statement, critical of decorative painting. The students were expelled and lecturers who defended them were dismissed (Elly Kent, Art and Australia, 2024).
The Biennale is auspiced by Dewan Kesenian Jakarta, the Jakarta Arts Council (Art and Australia).

Majelis Jakarta, an "open network of various art initiatives in Jakarta", has run it since 2024. The network began meeting in 2023 and its page lists 16 collectives (Jakarta Biennale website). NOW! Jakarta says 20 art collectives from Majelis Jakarta organised the 2024 edition.

The 2026 edition, "KEBAL", is artist-initiated. Its main exhibition runs 4 to 28 October 2026 at Taman Ismail Marzuki, Gedung Trisno Soemardjo, and programmes run 7 October to 24 November 2026 at collective spaces. The theme concerns residents "displaced" from Jakarta by rising property and living costs (Jakarta Biennale website).
Art and Australia says the collective ruangrupa implemented the Biennale for ten years.
details.funding_verdict: Jakarta Biennale: collective-run, auspiced by the Jakarta Arts Council
funding: Organiser: Majelis Jakarta, initiated by Dewan Kesenian Jakarta, the Jakarta Arts Council (NOW! Jakarta).

Art and Australia (Elly Kent, 2024) writes that publicly funded biennials depend on political will and key individuals rather than resilient institutions, and that government grant rounds failed to open in mid-2024.

press.overall: Two reviews of the 2024 edition criticise its curation and cohesion; they concern the exhibition, not its funders.

items.title: Innas Tsuroiya, "Jakarta Biennale 2024, '50 Tahun Jakarta Biennale 1974-2024'" (5 December 2024)
points: The decentralised method amounts to "un-curation"; the main exhibition lacks cohesion and gives little information about its curatorial framework.
Works are displayed without clear separation from other programmes, and many events were announced at short notice.
Judges the show "no greater than the sum of its parts" yet with notable moments, and argues the lumbung-inspired model could help new movements grow outside the metropolitan centres.

items.title: Elly Kent, "Contemporary Jakarta: A tale of two art events" (2024)
points: Criticises the 2024 Biennale for lacking cohesion: exhibition design gave visitors little help navigating the connections between works, and lighting, location and access undermined some strong works.
Argues biennials depend on key individuals rather than resilient institutions and succession planning.

details.bottom_line: The Jakarta Biennale has been organised since 2024 by Majelis Jakarta, an artist-collective network initiated by the Jakarta Arts Council, which auspices the Biennale (Art and Australia). Art and Australia reports that government grant rounds failed to open in mid-2024.

name: Museum Nasional Indonesia
funding: The pages read name the Indonesia Heritage Agency as the body restoring the museum after the fire of 16 September 2023 and give no budget, cost or funder amounts.
watch: Indonesia's national museum in Jakarta, reopened on 15 October 2024 after a fire on 16 September 2023 damaged Building A. Its reopening show presents more than 2,500 repatriated objects, about 300 returned from the Netherlands between 1978 and 2023.
records_note: No accounts were found in the pages read.

overview: A national museum on Jalan Medan Merdeka Barat, Central Jakarta, whose Building A was damaged by fire on 16 September 2023 (The Star, 19 Sep 2023).
The pages read give no founding date; it reopened to the public on 15 October 2024 after a year closed for restoration (The Art Newspaper, 15 Oct 2024).

What is there: the main exhibition presents more than 2,500 repatriated historical and cultural objects, of which about 1,750 were returned to Indonesia between 1977 and 2019 and 760 in 2023 and 2024; the total collection size is not stated in the pages read (The Art Newspaper, 15 Oct 2024).

Returns from the Netherlands, which colonised Indonesia from 1602 to 1949, were roughly 300 selected collections between 1978 and 2023, among them the Lombok treasure (July 2023), the Pita Maha Collection of 1930s Balinese painting, held at the Tropenmuseum in Amsterdam since the 1950s, and the Singhasari statues (The Art Newspaper, 15 Oct 2024).
Archive: the pages read say nothing of an archive or library.
details.funding_verdict: Museum Nasional Indonesia: state museum, funded through the Indonesia Heritage Agency; no budget figures found
funding: The Indonesia Heritage Agency announced the restoration; its acting head, Ahmad Mahendra, said full restoration will take three years (The Art Newspaper, 15 Oct 2024).
No reporting found, in the pages read, of the cost of the repairs, the budget of the museum or any private sponsor.

red_flags.heading: Fire
points: A fire on Saturday 16 September 2023 from about 8 p.m. lasted roughly three hours and damaged six rooms in Building A; an unnamed official said most of the items destroyed were replicas (The Star, 19 Sep 2023, citing The Jakarta Post).

The museum put on a companion show, Beating Nekara, Watering the Fire, that it said aims to answer public curiosity about the fire (The Art Newspaper, 15 Oct 2024). The cause is not stated in the pages read.

red_flags.heading: Colonial-era holdings
points: The museum's reopening show is built on objects returned from the Netherlands and elsewhere; Indonesia's coordinating minister for human development and culture, Muhadjir Effendy, attended the reopening ceremony (The Art Newspaper, 15 Oct 2024).

details.bottom_line: The pages read show a state museum run through the Indonesia Heritage Agency, with no funding figures. What to watch: the cost of restoring Building A and the three-year timetable.
details.website: https://museumnasional.or.id (not opened; no page of the site was read)

name: Ruang MES 56
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Artist collective in Yogyakarta that develops photography and contemporary art through a critical, contextual approach (Good News from Indonesia, 20 October 2026).
Formed in 2002. Wimo Ambala Bayang co-founded it with friends from ISI, the Indonesian Art Institute in Yogyakarta, and remains an active member (oddweb.org biographies).

Art Asia Pacific calls it Indonesia's first contemporary photography collective. Its members are predominantly male, and many studied at the Indonesian Institute of the Arts, the first school in the country to offer a photography degree.
The name MES 56 comes from the address of the group's first outpost (Art Asia Pacific, 13 April 2017).
The collective runs a house that serves as a studio, an educational space, a playground and a place to live (oddweb.org; Good News from Indonesia).
Programmes include workshops, discussions, communal and individual projects, and art residencies for young photography-based artists (Mayanga Anggrian, Jurnal Imajinasi, 2018).

Exhibitions: "The History of Boys: The MES 56 and Beyond" at DECK, Singapore, with eight MES photographers and three non-members, on view until 23 April 2017 (Art Asia Pacific). "Foam X Ruang Mes 56" at Foam, Amsterdam, 15 September to 12 November 2017 (photography-now.com). "Di Atas Hitam dan Putih" with 17 members at EDSU House, Sleman, from 16 October 2026 to 3 January 2027 (Good News from Indonesia).
details.funding_verdict: Ruang MES 56 (Yogyakarta): self-funded: the collective's own money and programmes
funding: Formed in 2002 with self-funding (oddweb.org biographies).
The collective has run programmes to sustain itself independently for more than fifteen years (exhibition listing on photography-now.com, 2017).
details.bottom_line: The money behind the collective is its own: oddweb.org says it was formed in 2002 with self-funding, and photography-now.com says its programmes have sustained it independently for more than fifteen years.

name: Selasar Sunaryo Art Space
funding: Founded 1998 by artist Sunaryo with direction and support from the Selasar Sunaryo Foundation.
records_note: A 2010 ASEF profile names only the Selasar Sunaryo Foundation.
affiliations_note: Selasar Sunaryo Art Space was set up in 1998 by the artist Sunaryo with direction and support from the Selasar Sunaryo Foundation.

overview: Non-profit art space on Jalan Bukit Pakar Timur, in the Dago area of Bandung (CNN Indonesia, detikTravel, culture360).

Founded by the artist Sunaryo, a former lecturer at the art and design faculty of the Bandung Institute of Technology, and opened on 5 September 1998 with his show "Titik Nadir", in which his works were covered in black cloth, which Manual calls "a sombre expression of the grief and uncertainty" of the socio-political turmoil of the time (detikTravel for the date, Manual).
CNN Indonesia says Sunaryo wanted to make a public place where artists and the public could interact.
Site and building: Sunaryo bought about 5,000 square metres of land and built the space himself (CNN Indonesia).

What is there: four exhibition rooms, each with a guide, and a cafe (detikTravel). Hundreds of exhibitions, workshops and residencies since opening (Manual). A programme guided by a council of academics, critics and art practitioners (culture360).

Visiting: Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 17:00. Ticket Rp 35,000 (detikTravel). CNN Indonesia reported free entry in 2017 and described two exhibition rooms. The Manual feature said an inclusive programme for disabled visitors is a future priority.
details.funding_verdict: Selasar Sunaryo Art Space: self-funded: the founder's land and building, backed by his foundation
funding: culture360 says it was founded in 1998 "with direction and support from the Selasar Sunaryo Foundation" and calls it a non-profit; the profile was posted on 6 September 2010 and names only that foundation.

The 25th-anniversary exhibition in 2023 included work by Sunaryo, his son Arin Dwihartanto Sunaryo and his daughter-in-law Syagini Ratna Wulan (Manual), so the founder's family is part of the programme.

press.overall: Very little criticism. The pieces found are descriptive or admiring and treat individual shows, not the institution or its money.

items.title: Tanya Michele Amador, "Selasar Sunaryo Art Space in Bandung Turns 20" (2018)
points: Calls the space an artist-run initiative with a distinctive place in Bandung for nurturing and engaging young artists after twenty years, and says the performance and installation work was the strength of the anniversary show.
Finds Sunaryo's stitched, patched abstract canvases deliberate and skilled, "certainly not an amateur" work.
Mostly celebratory; it does not discuss funding or governance.

items.title: Anindito Ariwandono, "Reconnecting with earth at Leuwigoèng" (2022)
points: Reviews the group show "Pulang Pada Tanah" ("Home to Soil") at Selasar Sunaryo; a photo caption notes some works are "rather raw in terms of their treatment".
Criticises the treatment of some works, not the institution.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the space is the founder's own: Sunaryo bought the land and built it, with a foundation behind it, and no sponsor or state funder is reported. The weak points are that no accounts, donors or board are published and that the founder's family shows work in the programme. Worth watching: whether a funder list or accounts are ever published.

name: Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art (TMoCA)
funding: State museum owned by the arts deputy of Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, which OFAC lists as an entity. The state set a 16.5 billion toman renovation budget.
watch: After 1979 the state kept its Western collection in storage. In 2017 the culture minister cancelled its Berlin and Rome loan show.
why_flagged: State museum owned by the arts deputy of Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, which OFAC lists as an entity. The state set a 16.5 billion toman renovation budget.
records_note: Its site only names the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance as the owner.

overview: State museum of modern and contemporary art next to Laleh Park in Tehran (Wikipedia).
Opened on 14 October 1977 (22 Mehr 1356) under Empress Farah Pahlavi, whose office oversaw art selection, funded by the National Iranian Oil Company (Wikipedia).
Designed by Kamran Diba with Nader Ardalan, mostly underground, with a spiral walkway and branching galleries (Wikipedia).
Holds more than 3,000 items: 19th and 20th century Western paintings, prints, drawings and sculpture, and a major collection of Iranian modern and contemporary art (Wikipedia).
After the 1979 revolution the Western works were kept in the vault. The first post-revolution exhibition of them was in 1999, and most are rarely shown (Wikipedia).

Closed for renovation in spring 2018 and reopened in early 2021 (Persian Wikipedia). A later show, "Eye to Eye", displayed over 120 Western works, with tickets costing about 14 US cents (Associated Press).
Head of the museum since April-May 2025: Reza Dabiri-Nejad (Persian Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art: state-owned and state-funded: Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance
funding: The museum is a unit of the Deputy for Arts Affairs of the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance (Persian Wikipedia).

The ministry allocated funding for the renovation in 1396 (2017-18). The official cost of the whole renovation project was 16.5 billion toman; in late 2018 officials said 5 billion had been spent and 3 billion more was needed (Etemad Online, January 2021).

red_flags.heading: Sanctions
points: The Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, the museum's owner, is on the US Specially Designated Nationals list: OFAC's recent-actions page of 8 November 2012 lists it under the IRAN-TRA program tag, and the Federal Register notice of 16 November 2012 ties the designations to Executive Order 13628 (OFAC, Federal Register).

red_flags.heading: State censorship
points: On 27 December 2016 the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, for the Berlin State Museums, cancelled a show of 61 works from the collection because Iran had not granted export permits; the show had been due to open on 4 December (Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, The Art Newspaper).

In February 2017 Culture Minister Reza Salehi-Amiri said he had proposed cancelling the Berlin and Rome loan show pending review, citing legal ambiguity in the agreement. The works were shown in Tehran in March 2017 instead (Tehran Times, 8 March 2017).
Iranian newspapers speculated the works would not return if they left Iran, and some officials who disapprove of art questioned the value of the show (The Art Newspaper).
Associated Press says Shiite clerics packed the museum's Western art into its vault after 1979, and that a Warhol print of the empress was slashed during the revolution.

press.overall: Little criticism of the museum itself; coverage centres on the 2016 cancellation of the Berlin loan show.

items.title: Catherine Hickley, "Berlin cancels show of Tehran's Modern art" (2016)
points: Iranian authorities missed the German deadline for export permits for works by Picasso, Pollock, Rothko and Bacon; Hermann Parzinger said further delays "couldn't be justified".
Treats the cancellation as a setback for German-Iranian relations after the 2015 nuclear deal.

items.outlet: Associated Press (news agency, not art press)
items.title: "Iran's much long hidden collection of Western art re-emerges despite high tensions with US" (undated copy on Ynetnews)
points: Describes the vaulted Western collection and the "Eye to Eye" show; quotes curator Jamal Arabzadeh and visitors; no official is quoted.

details.bottom_line: The money behind TMoCA is the Iranian state: the museum belongs to a ministry that OFAC listed on 8 November 2012. The documented weak point is state control of the collection, shown by the vaulting after 1979 and the 2016 to 2017 loan-show cancellation. Worth watching: how the Western works are shown and whether any foreign loan is allowed again.

name: Habima Theatre
funding: The pages read did not state Habima's budget. Jewish News (14 November 2016) reported that under Culture Minister Miri Regev, theatres that perform in settlements get a 10 percent bonus and those that refuse can face a one-third cut in government funding.
watch: Israel's national theatre, in Tel Aviv. It performed in Kiryat Arba on 10 November 2016 to Regev's praise; the 2010 boycott row over the Ariel centre that the pages read describe concerned the Beersheva company, not Habima.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: The Israeli national theatre company and its house in Tel Aviv.
The pages read did not give a founding date or the building's history.
What is there: the house and company; Habima staged Agnon's A Simple Story in Kiryat Arba on 10 November 2016 (Jewish News, 14 November 2016). No repertoire list was read.
Archive: the pages read did not describe one.
details.funding_verdict: Habima Theatre: state-funded in the pages read; amounts not found.
funding: Jewish News (14 November 2016): under Miri Regev, Israel's culture minister, theatres and cultural organisations that perform in settlements receive a 10 percent bonus and those that refuse can face a one-third cut in government funding.
No reporting found, in the pages read, of Habima's budget or private donors.

red_flags.heading: Settlement performances
points: On 10 November 2016 Habima played A Simple Story in Kiryat Arba, near Hebron; supporters of the theatre and left-wing groups opposed it, and one actor refused for ideological reasons (Jewish News, 14 November 2016).

Breaking the Silence took some of the actors on a tour of Hebron beforehand; Regev posted 'Well done, Habima. Well done, Kiryat Arba. Together we have made history' and said more shows would follow in Kiryat Arba, Bet El, Elkana and Ariel (Jewish News, 14 November 2016). The article carried no statement from Habima.

JTA (9 November 2010) reported a boycott row over the new Ariel arts centre involving the Beersheva Theater Company; Foreign Minister Avigdor Lieberman and Culture Minister Limor Livnat proposed funding sanctions on boycotting artists, and the Ariel shows went ahead. This concerned the Beersheva company, not Habima.

details.bottom_line: The pages read tie Habima to the culture ministry's funding rules for settlement performances, not to named donors or amounts. No dated 2022 to 2026 story was read.

name: Gallerie d'Italia
funding: Owned and funded by Intesa Sanpaolo through its Progetto Cultura.
watch: About 30 Extinction Rebellion activists occupied the Turin site on 2 March 2025 over owner Intesa Sanpaolo's investments. One institution, four sites.
why_flagged: Owned and funded by Intesa Sanpaolo through its Progetto Cultura.
records_note: It posts nothing itself; owner Intesa Sanpaolo posts annual reports and accounts for 2007 to 2025 and names its board, with no donor list.
affiliations_note: Gallerie d'Italia is a four-museum network of Intesa Sanpaolo, with sister museums in Naples, Turin and Vicenza besides Milan.

overview: Museum network owned by the bank Intesa Sanpaolo, with sites in Milan, Naples, Turin and Vicenza (Italian Wikipedia).

Vicenza, in Palazzo Leoni Montanari, opened in 1999. Milan opened on 3 November 2011 in Piazza della Scala. Turin opened on 17 May 2022 in Piazza San Carlo. Naples moved from Palazzo Zevallos to the Palazzo del Banco di Napoli on via Toledo on 21 May 2022 (Italian Wikipedia).

Milan joins three buildings: Palazzo Brentani, Palazzo Anguissola Antona Traversi and the former Banca Commerciale Italiana headquarters (stated by the space). Michele De Lucchi designed the Naples layout (Italian Wikipedia).

Milan shows 19th-century art, including Fondazione Cariplo's collection, the "Cantiere del '900" and an open store in the old vault. Turin focuses on photography and holds the Publifoto archive. Naples has Caravaggio's "Martirio di sant'Orsola" (stated by the space; Italian Wikipedia).
Michele Coppola is general director of the Gallerie and runs Intesa Sanpaolo's Progetto Cultura (Intesa Sanpaolo).

Milan opens Tuesday to Sunday, 9:30am to 7pm. €6 full, €3 reduced, free for under-26s, school groups and Intesa Sanpaolo customers. It runs programmes for visitors with motor, cognitive and sensory disabilities (stated by the space).
funding: Owned and run by Intesa Sanpaolo under its Progetto Cultura, conceived by Giovanni Bazoli, now honorary chairman, and part of a business plan that commits €1.5 billion to Italian communities by 2027 (Intesa Sanpaolo).
The four museums drew more than 750,000 visitors in 2024, a figure stated by the bank.

red_flags.heading: Owner's fossil fuel finance
points: ReCommon, an environmental group, reported in April 2025 that Intesa's lending to coal, oil and gas rose 18% in 2024 to about $11 billion and its investments rose 16% to about $10 billion, with ENI the top client (L'Indipendente). These are ReCommon's figures.

red_flags.heading: Extinction Rebellion occupation in Turin
points: On 2 March 2025, the last day of the "American Nature" show, about 30 Extinction Rebellion activists entered with tickets and lay down in the room on fossil fuel damage, protesting the "harmful investments" of Intesa Sanpaolo, the museum's owner (LaPresse).

red_flags.heading: Privacy fines against the owner
points: Italy's data protection authority fined Intesa Sanpaolo €31.8 million after an employee made more than 6,600 unjustified accesses to the data of 3,573 customers between February 2022 and April 2024, some of them public figures (QuiFinanza, March 2026).
In March 2026 the same authority fined it €17.6 million for unlawfully processing the data of about 2.4 million customers moved to Isybank (Il Post).

press.overall: The Extinction Rebellion action was covered by the general press, not the art press.

details.bottom_line: The museums are a bank's own cultural programme, paid for by Intesa Sanpaolo with no separate budget published. The weak points are the bank's fossil fuel lending, which drew a protest inside the Turin museum in 2025, and two 2026 privacy fines. Worth watching: whether the Turin site's climate shows keep attracting protest aimed at the owner.

name: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli
funding: A state museum; the pages read did not state its budget or funders, and its site links an annual report and a support-us page.
watch: Home of the Farnese, Egyptian, Pompeii, epigraphic and numismatic collections. In July 2025 Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli named Francesco Sirano its director in a late-night announcement of five directors; Paolo Giulierini had been reconfirmed director in July 2019.
records_note: Its site links an annual report, strategic plan, museum charter and transparency pages.

overview: A national archaeological museum at Piazza Museo 18/19, Naples (museum website).

What is there: on display the Farnese collection and the Farnese gems, an Egyptian collection, Pompeii material (furnishings, a scale model of Pompeii, frescoes), an epigraphic collection and a numismatic collection; the Mosaic section and the Secret Cabinet are closed for refurbishment until further notice and the Mosaic of Alexander is under restoration (museum website).
Archive: the site lists a library and a photographic archive under scientific services; the page read gives no holdings (museum website).
In 2018 the museum reported 613,000 visitors, up 16.7 percent on 2017 (Finestre sull'Arte, 27 July 2019).
details.funding_verdict: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli: public, a state museum; amounts not stated in the pages read.
funding: The site has no funding figures; it links to an annual report, strategic plan and a support-us page (museum website).
No reporting found in the pages read of the Ministry's grant, ticket income or sponsors.

red_flags.heading: Governance
points: On 16 July 2025 Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli announced the directors of five major state museums late at night, among them Francesco Sirano for the MANN, a ministry official who had directed the Ercolano archaeological park (Artribune, July 2025).

Finestre sull'Arte wrote on 17 July 2025 that Giuli, according to an unpublished Corriere della Sera interview he shared on social media, was not satisfied with the shortlists proposed by the selection commission and was ready to reopen the call; he made the appointments anyway (Finestre sull'Arte, 17 July 2025).
Giulierini had been reconfirmed as MANN director for four more years, announced by director general Antonio Lampis at the museum's annual report in July 2019 (Finestre sull'Arte, 27 July 2019).

details.bottom_line: The State pays and appoints, and the 2025 director change was announced by the minister over a shortlist he was reported to be unhappy with. The pages read give no budget figures.

name: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Reggio Calabria (MArRC)
funding: The museum site sits on the Ministry of Culture's cultura.gov.it domain. The pages read did not state its budget or funders.
watch: State archaeological museum in Piazza De Nava, Reggio Calabria, home of the Riace Bronzes.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The pages read did not link published accounts.

overview: Archaeological museum at Piazza De Nava 26, Reggio di Calabria (museum website).

What is there: five levels labelled A to E, including level D, "From ancient Reggio to the Riace Bronzes", and a dedicated Riace Bronzes section (museum website). The pages read did not give an object count.
Archive: the site has a library page under Education; the pages read did not describe its holdings (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Reggio Calabria (MArRC): state museum; the pages read did not state amounts
funding: Hosted on the Ministry of Culture's domain; the pages read did not state the budget or any funder.
No reporting found of sponsors or income in the pages read.
details.bottom_line: The pages read do not show how the museum is paid for. Its accounts and the Ministry's allocation are the pages to find.
